items.title: 5.5 Equation of Lines Through the Point of Intersection of Two Lines

source_refs.note: Book pp. 149-153: 5.5 family of lines l1 + k l2 = 0, Example 11 (a), (b), Theorems 4-6 (altitudes, right bisectors, medians concurrent) with Figures 5.5-5.7.

blocks.text:
We can find a family of lines through the point of intersection of two non-parallel lines \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\). Let
\[\ell_1 : a_1x + b_1y + c_1 = 0 \quad \ldots(i)\]
and
\[\ell_2 : a_2x + b_2y + c_2 = 0 \quad \ldots(ii)\]

For a non-zero real \(k\), consider the equation
\[a_1x + b_1y + c_1\]
\[+ k(a_2x + b_2y + c_2) = 0 \;\ldots(iii)\]
This, being a linear equation, represents a straight line. For different values of \(k\), (iii) represents different lines. Thus (iii) is a family of lines.

If \((x_1, y_1)\) is any point lying on both (i) and (ii), then it is their point of intersection. Since, \((x_1, y_1)\) lies on both (i) and (ii), we have
\[a_1x_1 + b_1y_1 + c_1 = 0\]
and
\[a_2x_1 + b_2y_1 + c_2 = 0\]
From the above two equations, we note that \((x_1, y_1)\) also lies on (iii).
Thus, (iii) is the required family of lines through the point of intersection of (i) and (ii). Since, \(k\) can assume an infinite number of values, (iii) represents an infinite number of lines.
A particular line of the family (iii) can be determined if one more condition is given.

blocks.text_alt: l1 plus k times l2 equals zero

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does \((x_1, y_1)\) lie on (iii)? Put it in the left side of (iii): it becomes \(0 + k \cdot 0 = 0\). So every member of the family passes through the meeting point, whatever \(k\) is.
Why is (iii) a line? Collect terms: \((a_1 + ka_2)x + (b_1 + kb_2)y + (c_1 + kc_2) = 0\), which is first degree in \(x\) and \(y\). (The coefficients of \(x\) and \(y\) cannot both be zero, because that would make \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) parallel.)
Why is this useful? We find the required line without first finding the point of intersection: we only need one more condition (parallel, perpendicular, through a point, ...) to fix \(k\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Small detail: \(k = 0\) gives \(\ell_1\) itself, but no value of \(k\) gives \(\ell_2\). So if the required line happens to be \(\ell_2\), the equation for \(k\) will have no solution; then check \(\ell_2\) directly.

blocks.title: Example 11
blocks.problem:
Find the family of lines through the point of intersection of the lines \(2x - 3y - 14 = 0\) and \(2x + y - 10 = 0\). Find the member of the family which is:
(a) parallel to the line with slope \(-\frac{1}{2}\)
(b) perpendicular to the line \(2x - 3y + 2 = 0\)
steps:
Given: \(2x - 3y - 14 = 0\) ...(i) and \(2x + y - 10 = 0\) ...(ii).
To find: the family of lines through their point of intersection, and the members (a) with slope \(-\frac{1}{2}\) (parallel), (b) perpendicular to \(2x - 3y + 2 = 0\).
Method: write the family \(\ell_1 + k\ell_2 = 0\), find its slope in terms of \(k\), then use the slope condition (\(m_1 = m_2\) for parallel, \(m_1m_2 = -1\) for perpendicular) to find \(k\).

Write the family
A family of lines through the point of intersection of equations (i) and (ii) is:
\[2x - 3y - 14 + k(2x + y - 10) = 0\]
\[(2 + 2k)x + (k - 3)y\]
\[+ (-14 - 10k) = 0 \;\ldots(iii)\]
Why: \(\ell_1 + k\ell_2 = 0\) passes through the meeting point for every \(k\). Collecting the \(x\) terms, the \(y\) terms and the constants gives the general form.

Slope of the family
Slope of (iii) is given by:
\[m = -\dfrac{2 + 2k}{k - 3}\]
Why: the slope of \(ax + by + c = 0\) is \(-\frac{a}{b}\); here \(a = 2 + 2k\) and \(b = k - 3\). This is the slope of any member of the family (iii).

(a) Parallel: equate the slopes
If (iii) is parallel to the line with slope \(-\frac{1}{2}\), then
\[-\dfrac{2 + 2k}{k - 3} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\]
\[4 + 4k = k - 3\]
\[3k = -7\]
\[k = -\dfrac{7}{3}\]
Why: parallel lines have equal slopes. Cross-multiplying \(\frac{2 + 2k}{k - 3} = \frac{1}{2}\) gives \(2(2 + 2k) = k - 3\).

(a) Put \(k = -\frac{7}{3}\) in (iii)
\[\left(2 + 2\left(-\tfrac{7}{3}\right)\right)x + \left(-\tfrac{7}{3} - 3\right)y\]
\[+ \left(-14 - 10\left(-\tfrac{7}{3}\right)\right) = 0\]
\[\left(\tfrac{6 - 14}{3}\right)x + \left(\tfrac{-7 - 9}{3}\right)y + \left(\tfrac{-42 + 70}{3}\right) = 0\]
\[-\tfrac{8}{3}x - \tfrac{16}{3}y + \tfrac{28}{3} = 0\]
\[-8x - 16y + 28 = 0\]
\[2x + 4y - 7 = 0\]
Why: substitute in each coefficient, simplify each bracket over the denominator 3, multiply by 3, then divide by \(-4\) to get the simplest form. This is the required equation of the member of the family.

(b) Perpendicular: product of slopes is \(-1\)
Slope of \(2x - 3y + 2 = 0\) ...(iv) is \(\frac{2}{3}\). Since (iii) is perpendicular to (iv), we have
\[-\dfrac{2 + 2k}{k - 3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} = -1\]
\[4 + 4k = 3k - 9\]
\[k = -13\]
Why: \(m_1m_2 = -1\) for perpendicular lines. The left side simplifies to \(-\frac{2(2 + 2k)}{3(k - 3)} = -1\), so \(2(2 + 2k) = 3(k - 3)\).

Check:
Lines (i) and (ii) meet at \(\left(\frac{11}{2}, -1\right)\) (subtract (ii) from (i): \(-4y = 4\)).
\[2\left(\tfrac{11}{2}\right) + 4(-1) - 7 = 0\]
\[6\left(\tfrac{11}{2}\right) + 4(-1) - 29 = 0\]
Slopes: \(2x + 4y - 7 = 0\) has slope \(-\frac{1}{2}\); \(6x + 4y - 29 = 0\) has slope \(-\frac{3}{2}\), and \(-\frac{3}{2} \times \frac{2}{3} = -1\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Theorems 4, 5 and 6 below use one idea three times: write the three special lines of a triangle in general form, apply Theorem 3, and add the second and third rows to the first row. The first row becomes all zeros, so the determinant is zero and the lines are concurrent.
Theorem 4
Altitudes of a triangle are concurrent.

blocks.alt: Triangle A(x1, y1), B(x2, y2), C(x3, y3) with magenta sides on a pale yellow panel; its three altitudes AD, BE and CF in cyan, each with a black right-angle mark at its foot, meet at the point O.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.5: The altitudes AD, BE and CF of triangle ABC meet at O (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.5)

blocks.text:
Proof: Let the coordinates of the vertices of \(\triangle ABC\) be as shown in figure. Then, slope of \(\overline{BC} = \frac{y_2 - y_3}{x_2 - x_3}\). Therefore, slope of the altitude \(AD = -\frac{x_2 - x_3}{y_2 - y_3}\). Equation of the altitude \(AD\) is
\[y - y_1 = -\dfrac{x_2 - x_3}{y_2 - y_3}(x - x_1)\]
(point-slope form) or
\[x(x_2 - x_3) + y(y_2 - y_3)\]
\[- x_1(x_2 - x_3) - y_1(y_2 - y_3) = 0 \;\ldots(i)\]

Equations of the altitudes \(BE\) and \(CF\) are respectively (by symmetry)
\[x(x_3 - x_1) + y(y_3 - y_1)\]
\[- x_2(x_3 - x_1) - y_2(y_3 - y_1) = 0 \;\ldots(ii)\]
and
\[x(x_1 - x_2) + y(y_1 - y_2)\]
\[- x_3(x_1 - x_2) - y_3(y_1 - y_2) = 0 \;\ldots(iii)\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
'By symmetry' means: equation (ii) is obtained from (i) by moving every label one step round the triangle, \(1 \to 2\), \(2 \to 3\), \(3 \to 1\) (A to B, B to C, C to A). So the altitude from \(B\) is perpendicular to \(CA\) and passes through \((x_2, y_2)\).
Notice also that (i) says \((x - x_1)(x_2 - x_3) + (y - y_1)(y_2 - y_3) = 0\). In this form it is correct even when \(BC\) is horizontal or vertical (where the slope fraction would have a zero denominator), so the proof covers every triangle.

The three lines (i), (ii) and (iii) are concurrent if and only if
\[\begin{vmatrix} x_2 - x_3 & y_2 - y_3 & p_1 \\ x_3 - x_1 & y_3 - y_1 & p_2 \\ x_1 - x_2 & y_1 - y_2 & p_3 \end{vmatrix}\]
where \(p_1 = -x_1(x_2 - x_3) - y_1(y_2 - y_3)\), \(p_2 = -x_2(x_3 - x_1) - y_2(y_3 - y_1)\) and \(p_3 = -x_3(x_1 - x_2) - y_3(y_1 - y_2)\) are the constant terms of (i), (ii) and (iii).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The book prints this determinant without '\(= 0\)' at the end. The condition of Theorem 3 is that the determinant equals zero: it should read
\[\begin{vmatrix} x_2 - x_3 & y_2 - y_3 & p_1 \\ x_3 - x_1 & y_3 - y_1 & p_2 \\ x_1 - x_2 & y_1 - y_2 & p_3 \end{vmatrix} = 0\]
(the very next line of the book does show \(= 0\)).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: To fit a phone screen we write the long third-column entries as \(p_1\), \(p_2\), \(p_3\); the book prints them in full. They are just the constant terms \(c\) of the three lines, exactly as in Theorem 3.

Adding \(2^{nd}\) and \(3^{rd}\) rows to the \(1^{st}\) row of the determinant, we have
\[\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ x_3 - x_1 & y_3 - y_1 & p_2 \\ x_1 - x_2 & y_1 - y_2 & p_3 \end{vmatrix} = 0\]
Thus, the altitudes of the triangle are concurrent.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why is the new first row all zeros? Column 1: \((x_2 - x_3) + (x_3 - x_1) + (x_1 - x_2) = 0\). Column 2 is the same with \(y\). Column 3: \(p_1 + p_2 + p_3 = 0\), because every product such as \(x_1x_2\) appears once with \(+\) and once with \(-\). Adding rows does not change the value of a determinant, and a determinant with a zero row is \(0\). The altitudes are never parallel (they are perpendicular to sides that are not parallel), so Theorem 3 applies. The common point \(O\) of the altitudes is called the orthocentre (this name is ours, not printed here).
Theorem 5
Right bisectors of a triangle are concurrent.

blocks.alt: Triangle A(x1, y1), B(x2, y2), C(x3, y3) with magenta sides on a pale yellow panel; the right bisectors of the sides, drawn in cyan from the midpoints D, E, F (coordinates written as fractions) with black right-angle marks, meet at the point O.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.6: The right bisectors of the sides of triangle ABC meet at O (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.6)

blocks.text:
Proof: Let \(A(x_1, y_1)\), \(B(x_2, y_2)\) and \(C(x_3, y_3)\) be the vertices of \(\triangle ABC\). The mid-point \(D\) of \(BC\) has coordinates \(\left(\frac{x_2 + x_3}{2}, \frac{y_2 + y_3}{2}\right)\). Since the slope of \(\overline{BC}\) is \(\frac{y_2 - y_3}{x_2 - x_3}\), the slope of the right bisector \(DO\) of \(BC\) is \(-\frac{x_2 - x_3}{y_2 - y_3}\).
Equation of the right bisector \(DO\) of \(BC\) is:
\[y - \dfrac{y_2 + y_3}{2}\]
\[= -\dfrac{x_2 - x_3}{y_2 - y_3}\left(x - \dfrac{x_2 + x_3}{2}\right)\]
(By using, point-slope form) or
\[x(x_2 - x_3) + y(y_2 - y_3)\]
\[- \tfrac{1}{2}(y_2^2 - y_3^2) - \tfrac{1}{2}(x_2^2 - x_3^2) = 0\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The book does not number this first equation, but in the next lines it calls it (i). Getting it: multiply both sides by \(y_2 - y_3\), bring everything to one side, and use \(\left(y - \frac{y_2 + y_3}{2}\right)(y_2 - y_3) = y(y_2 - y_3) - \frac{1}{2}(y_2^2 - y_3^2)\) (difference of squares); the \(x\) part works the same way.

By symmetry, equations of the other two right bisectors \(EO\) and \(FO\) are respectively:
\[x(x_3 - x_1) + y(y_3 - y_1)\]
\[- \tfrac{1}{2}(y_3^2 - y_1^2) - \tfrac{1}{2}(x_3^2 - x_1^2) = 0 \;\ldots(ii)\]
and
\[x(x_1 - x_2) + y(y_1 - y_2)\]
\[- \tfrac{1}{2}(y_1^2 - y_2^2) - \tfrac{1}{2}(x_1^2 - x_2^2) = 0 \;\ldots(iii)\]

The lines (i), (ii) and (iii) will be concurrent if and only if
\[\begin{vmatrix} x_2 - x_3 & y_2 - y_3 & q_1 \\ x_3 - x_1 & y_3 - y_1 & q_2 \\ x_1 - x_2 & y_1 - y_2 & q_3 \end{vmatrix} = 0\]
where \(q_1 = -\frac{1}{2}(y_2^2 - y_3^2) - \frac{1}{2}(x_2^2 - x_3^2)\), \(q_2 = -\frac{1}{2}(y_3^2 - y_1^2) - \frac{1}{2}(x_3^2 - x_1^2)\) and \(q_3 = -\frac{1}{2}(y_1^2 - y_2^2) - \frac{1}{2}(x_1^2 - x_2^2)\) are the constant terms.

Adding \(2^{nd}\) and \(3^{rd}\) row to \(1^{st}\) row of the determinant, we have
\[\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ x_3 - x_1 & y_3 - y_1 & q_2 \\ x_1 - x_2 & y_1 - y_2 & q_3 \end{vmatrix} = 0\]
Thus, the right bisectors of a triangle are concurrent.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Again each column adds up to zero: in column 3, \(y_2^2 - y_3^2 + y_3^2 - y_1^2 + y_1^2 - y_2^2 = 0\), and the same for the \(x^2\) terms. The common point \(O\) is the same distance from \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) (every point of a right bisector is equidistant from the two ends of that side), so it is the centre of the circle through the three vertices, called the circumcentre (our addition).
Theorem 6
Medians of the triangle are concurrent.

blocks.alt: Triangle A(x1, y1), B(x2, y2), C(x3, y3) with magenta sides on a pale yellow panel; the medians AD, BE and CF in cyan go to the midpoints D, E, F (coordinates written as fractions) and meet at the point O.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.7: The medians AD, BE and CF of triangle ABC meet at O (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.7)

blocks.text:
Proof: Let \(A(x_1, y_1)\), \(B(x_2, y_2)\) and \(C(x_3, y_3)\) be the vertices of \(\triangle ABC\). The mid-point \(D\) of \(BC\) has coordinates \(\left(\frac{x_2 + x_3}{2}, \frac{y_2 + y_3}{2}\right)\).
Equation of the median \(AD\) is
\[\dfrac{y - y_1}{\frac{y_2 + y_3}{2} - y_1} = \dfrac{x - x_1}{\frac{x_2 + x_3}{2} - x_1}\]
(Two-point form) or
\[x(y_2 + y_3 - 2y_1)\]
\[+ y(2x_1 - x_2 - x_3)\]
\[- x_1(y_2 + y_3 - 2y_1)\]
\[+ y_1(x_2 + x_3 - 2x_1) = 0 \;\ldots(i)\]

By symmetry, equations of the other two medians \(BE\) and \(CF\) are respectively:
\[x(y_3 + y_1 - 2y_2)\]
\[+ y(2x_2 - x_3 - x_1)\]
\[- x_2(y_3 + y_1 - 2y_2)\]
\[+ y_2(x_3 + x_1 - 2x_2) = 0 \;\ldots(ii)\]
\[x(y_1 + y_2 - 2y_3)\]
\[+ y(2x_3 - x_1 - x_2)\]
\[- x_3(y_1 + y_2 - 2y_3)\]
\[+ y_3(x_1 + x_2 - 2x_3) = 0 \;\ldots(iii)\]

The lines (i), (ii) and (iii) will be concurrent if and only if
\[\begin{vmatrix} y_2 + y_3 - 2y_1 & 2x_1 - x_2 - x_3 & r_1 \\ y_3 + y_1 - 2y_2 & 2x_2 - x_3 - x_1 & r_2 \\ y_1 + y_2 - 2y_3 & 2x_3 - x_1 - x_2 & r_3 \end{vmatrix} = 0\]
where \(r_1\), \(r_2\), \(r_3\) are the constant terms of (i), (ii), (iii): \(r_1 = -x_1(y_2 + y_3 - 2y_1) + y_1(x_2 + x_3 - 2x_1)\), and \(r_2\), \(r_3\) in the same way.

Adding \(2^{nd}\) and \(3^{rd}\) row to \(1^{st}\) row, we have
\[\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ y_3 + y_1 - 2y_2 & 2x_2 - x_3 - x_1 & r_2 \\ y_1 + y_2 - 2y_3 & 2x_3 - x_1 - x_2 & r_3 \end{vmatrix} = 0\]
Thus, the medians of a triangle are concurrent.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
From the two-point form to (i): multiply both fractions' denominators by 2 and cross-multiply: \((y - y_1)(x_2 + x_3 - 2x_1) = (x - x_1)(y_2 + y_3 - 2y_1)\), then bring everything to one side.
The common point of the medians is the centroid, \(\left(\frac{x_1 + x_2 + x_3}{3}, \frac{y_1 + y_2 + y_3}{3}\right)\) (our addition; you can check it satisfies (i)).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Lines through the meeting point of \(\ell_1 = 0\) and \(\ell_2 = 0\): \(\ell_1 + k\ell_2 = 0\) (a family of lines).
2. One extra condition (parallel, perpendicular, through a point) fixes \(k\) and so one member of the family.
3. Slope of \((a_1 + ka_2)x + (b_1 + kb_2)y + \ldots = 0\) is \(-\frac{a_1 + ka_2}{b_1 + kb_2}\).
4. Altitudes, right bisectors and medians of every triangle are concurrent (Theorems 4, 5, 6).
5. Proof pattern: Theorem 3 plus adding rows 2 and 3 to row 1 to get a zero row.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing the family as \(\ell_1 + \ell_2 + k = 0\) or \(k\ell_1 = \ell_2\) with the constant in the wrong place: it must be \(\ell_1 + k\ell_2 = 0\), \(k\) multiplying the whole second expression.
2. Forgetting to multiply the constant term of \(\ell_2\) by \(k\) (for example writing \(-14 - 10\) instead of \(-14 - 10k\)).
3. Using \(m_1 = m_2\) for perpendicular lines or \(m_1m_2 = -1\) for parallel ones.
4. Using the slope of a side instead of the perpendicular slope for an altitude or a right bisector.
